The study of cosmic microwave background (CMB) anomalies is an active area of research that could be influenced by instrumental effects. While foreground removal methods can impact the results, the impact of biases in these methods is not well understood and may also contribute to these anomalies. Researchers require tools that simulate instrumental biases in CMB experiments to better comprehend potential limitations and improvements. Currently, available codes primarily focus on simulating noise and foregrounds in CMB data, without addressing biases. Consequently, researchers have developed a new Python code called s4cmb, which generates simulated datasets for experiments similar to South Pole Telescope and Simons Observatory, complete with noise, foregrounds, and biases that affect temperature and polarization cross-spectra. The code enables users to easily modify noise and foreground assumptions, as well as various bias sources, to better understand the effects of different assumptions on anomaly indicators. The simulation of bias sources includes systematic errors in temperature and polarization, as well as masking effects that influence beam convolution, foreground removal, and component separation. The researchers behind s4cmb intend for it to be a versatile tool that can be used in conjunction with existing codes, such as multipoles, Camb, and Camb Theatre, to simulate biases in other experiments. They also encourage other researchers to contribute to the code and explore the influence of instrumental biases on data analysis methods. The adoption of s4cmb can help validate and improve current experiments and provide valuable insights for future ones. The code is available for download on github dot com. The researchers behind s4cmb have used the code to simulate biases in experiments similar to CMB-S4, which could observe the anomalous dipole in the CMB, as well as to investigate the impact of beam convolution, foreground removal, and component separation on anomaly indicators. The simulation of beam convolution shows that instrumental biases can influence the shape of the anomalous dipole, while the impact of foreground removal and component separation on the dipole's amplitude is minimal. The researchers found that the bias in the dipole's amplitude is primarily caused by the removal of polarized foregrounds below $3\sigma$ thresholds, which could be corrected by improving the removal method or increasing the sensitivity to reduce the bias to an acceptable level. The simulation of polarized foregrounds also shows that the bias in the dipole's orientation is minimal, which is consistent with the results of previous studies. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable deepfake detection method. Based on the CSD-Net architecture, which combines feature stitching and spatial attention techniques to distinguish deepfakes, this study introduces a novel multi-domain cross-stitched network to enhance detection performance. By employing two separate stitching techniques, we differentiate between surface and feature-level fusion, thereby harnessing the unique strengths of each technique and mitigating potential drawbacks. Consequently, a comprehensive and versatile network is created, with increased resistance to various attack types and notable detection accuracy improvements, as validated through extensive experimentation on state-of-the-art evaluation benchmarks. Moreover, this study demonstrates how MD-CSDNetwork can be effectively fine-tuned for real-world applications, including the detection of face swapping and audio manipulation attacks. Compared to existing methods, our proposed framework achieves superior performance on various evaluation metrics, as evident from the reported results. The code is available online at https://github.com/ChengjunJiang/MD-CSDNetwork.

Fraudulent activities on the internet have a long and fascinating history, with scammers continually adapting new techniques to deceive victims. The rise of blockchain technology and decentralized applications has created a new environment where fraudulent schemes can thrive, leveraging advanced security features to conceal their true purposes. This research delves into the intricate workings of Forsage, a highly successful and widely promoted pseudosmart contract gambling application, to understand its operational mechanics and the financial gains of its perpetrators. By examining transaction data and interviewing participants, we gained a detailed insight into how Forsage's designers exploited vulnerabilities in the etherum network and broke multiple rules of the etherum platform, all while presenting a legitimate facade to thousands of victims. Despite an extensive investigation, we were unable to pinpoint the identities of the individuals behind Forsage, who are believed to have escaped with an estimated $265 million in stolen funds. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We have made the research data available for further public analysis.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two-component electron beam model can be interpreted as the superposition of bright flare kernels and weaker ribbons in a larger area. This analysis highlights the importance of pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, together with the significance of low-energy electrons in the far-ultraviolet continuum, Balmer line broadening, and the optical color temperature in stellar flares. This research was supported by the NASA HSR and ADIO programs.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for safety enhancement in critical engineering projects.
The potential for these materials to deteriorate and the extent of their damage are critical factors that need assessment.
A numerical model based on the Halpin-Kardos approximation represents the material's electrical conductivity and mechanical properties, accounting for the influence of fiber distribution, conductive nanofillers, and damage.
Genetic algorithms are utilized to calibrate the model, incorporating the results of Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) scans that map the material's conductivity and comparing them with the computed conductivity.
The assessed model then predicts the material's mechanical properties and damage distribution.
In a test involving impact loading, the calculated results compare favorably with actual data from EIT scans and mechanical tests.
However, discrepancies in the conducted and calculated conductivity, likely due to EIT's scan resolution, result in the genetic algorithm failing to converge fully.

The fundamental units of a system, referred to as elements, can either be highly sophisticated on their own or they can be simple and effective when working together as a whole. While this dichotomy may seem straightforward, research has shown that a system's elements can also be both complex and intelligent in their own right. However, when considering the broader context of a system that contains multiple elements, each with varying levels of internal complexity and intelligence, determining the level of intelligence exhibited by the system as a whole becomes more challenging. One possible approach to analyzing this type of system is through the lens of co-intelligence, which focuses on the interplay between different forms of intelligence within a system. Another strategy is to examine the system's components and the relationship between its internal complexity and external simplicity. By exploring these concepts, this talk will delve into the intricacies of a system comprised of multiple elements, each with its own unique level of complexity and intelligence, and examine various case studies that demonstrate the co-evolution of complex systems and their individual components. Furthermore, it will also discuss the implications of these findings for our understanding of how to effectively manage and govern these types of systems. Lastly, the talk will conclude by presenting a framework known as the "Intelligence Continuum," which provides a framework for analyzing the level of intelligence exhibited by a system's elements and offering guidance on how to promote the development of more intelligent systems. This talk is geared towards a diverse audience consisting of policymakers, technologists, biologists, and social scientists, with the goal of fostering a deeper understanding of the complex relationships that exist within systems and between their components and the environment, and exploring various strategies for promoting greater intelligence and coherence within these systems. This talk is based on the work of Stuart Umpleby, with additional input from other prominent researchers in the field. The talk will be delivered in an informal style, with ample opportunities for Q\&A sessions. The concepts to be presented include the distinction between internal and external complexity, the co-evolution of complex systems and their components, the importance of promoting diversity within these systems, and the role of governance in facilitating their development. The talk will also address various case studies and examples from biology, technology, and social sciences. The talk is divided into three main parts, with the first part focusing on the fundamental principles of co-intelligence, the second part examining the interplay between complexity and simplicity in different systems, and the third part exploring various strategies for promoting greater intelligence and coherence within these systems. The talk will be delivered over three hours

We investigate right-angled Artin complexes based on a graph whose edge labelling forms a partial order. A key result shows that a group G acting faithfully on a right-angled Artin complex acts freely if its action respects the edge labelling of the graph, provided there is no directed path in the graph with starting and ending vertices equal. Additionally, for a free group F_2, we find that any action on a right-angled Artin complex that respects the edge labelling will not be cocompact unless the graph consists of two unconnected vertices. Furthermore, in the scenario where the action is cocompact, we establish that the graph must be composed of at least two connected components, each containing at least one vertex. If the graph contains a directed cycle, we demonstrate that any action on the right-angled Artin complex is isomorphic to an action on a right-angled Artin complex defined by a modified graph without the cycle, along with an extension to include a central vertex in the center of the group. Lastly, we show that any action on a right-angled Artin complex resulting in a finite number of orbits can be equivalently studied using a graph with a finite number of directed paths. The research also explores an analogue of the Small-Potter theorem and a result on the action of a free group on a right-angled Artin complex defined by a graph with an infinite number of directed paths. Identifying the connections between interrelated time series data is crucial in many fields, including economics, neuroscience, and finance, where understanding these connections can inform about the behavior of individual time series, facilitate forecastings and provide early warning signals for potential crises. In recent years, connectivity estimation techniques have been largely static, failing to capture the ever-changing connections between time series in dynamic environments. This paper introduces a novel technique, called DeepDynam, a two-layer neural network model that automatically detects time-varying connections between interrelated time series without prespecifying the size of the underlying network. Unlike current approaches, this model's performance is validated through a range of simulation studies and real-world data sets, including macroeconomic indicators, financial stocks, and brain activity measurements, demonstrating the efficacy and generality of the approach. Furthermore, this model's efficiency and effectiveness are compared to state-of-the-art methods, revealing its superior performance in predicting connections and key variables of interest. This research is complemented by an open-source implementation of the model, along with guidance on incorporating regularization techniques and an interactive visualization dashboard for exploring the results. This technique and its implementation can serve as a foundation for a range of applications, including big data analysis, neuroscience research, and financial risk management. This research focuses on advancing the design of a monopod for heterogeneous terrain hopping by airdrop paratroopers. To achieve this, we developed a simulation framework consisting of three modules. The first module, which simulates the terrain, allows for heterogeneous terrain hopping scenarios and accounts for soil deformation under pressure and load. The second module, modeling the pilot's movements, uses a nonlinear control approach to track desired movement patterns despite uncertainties in the terrain. The third module, which controls the landing leg jump forces, employs a feedforward controller to ensure safe takeoff from the terrain. To validate the simulation and controller effectiveness, realistic terrain and pilot movement scenarios were created, and the simulation was expanded to include issues typically encountered in helicopter airdrops. These scenarios showed that the monopod's hopping capability can be effectively utilized to reduce the risk of digging into hard ground or getting stuck in soft ground. Furthermore, the simulation demonstrated that the pilot's movement patterns can be tailored to meet specific terrain hazards avoidance criteria, thus minimizing the risk of injury to the paratrooper. To facilitate practical application, suggestions have been provided for designing and refining the pilot's movement patterns based on simulation data. In this paper, the contact interaction model between mesons and gluons is applied to calculate the form factors of mesons. A comparison with the QCD sum rule method is made, and the two approaches are found to be compatible for mesons with a high quark mass, such as the $D$ and $B$ mesons. The contact interaction model facilitates the calculation of form factors for mesons with hidden charm or bottom quark components, which are difficult with the QCD sum rules method due to its high sensitivity to the Borel transformation parameter. The form factor values obtained using the contact interaction model are presented for various meson families, including those that aren't typically analyzed, like the $\bar{c}g$ and $\bar{b}g$ mesons. The decay constants of these mesons are also calculated and the results are compared with those found using the QCD sum rules method. The lifetime predictions for the $\bar{c}g$ and $\bar{b}g$ mesons, based on their decay widths, are discussed and the necessary contact interaction parameters are estimated. The paper also presents calculations for the electromagnetic form factors of light mesons, which are more challenging due to the small mass gap between the quark and gluon components. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the diverse structures and sizes of modern information networks. Presently, most techniques rely on rigid categorization models, neglecting the inherent relationships within networks, and often produce poorly performing and inefficient results. In contrast, we propose a novel approach that leverages topic modeling from the field of natural language processing to generate optimized hierarchies for real-world networks, outperforming existing methods in various evaluation metrics. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates significant improvements in scalability, enabling the efficient construction of high-quality hierarchies for large networks comprising numerous entities and interconnected topics. We illustrate the effectiveness of our method using a range of networks, including a sprawling Wikipedia database of over 79,000 categories. Our framework's open-source implementation is available for public use.

Quantum annealing within a suitable interval can lead to successful outcomes, but the origins of this quantum annealing window are not well understood. This study investigates the quantum annealing window in the exact cover problem using quantum quench dynamics and quantum phase structure. It finds that the inner edges of the quantum annealing window coincide with the onset of localization due to classical chaos, and the outer edges are influenced by the presence of multiple ground state connections to the initial state. This research also demonstrates that modifying the quantum annealing trajectory can result in a larger quantum annealing window, and that intermittent failures in annealing can occur in the absence of initial condition dependence, driven by random fluctuations in the initial state. This behavior is distinct from reports of occasional failures in other contexts, where initial condition dependence was observed. It is possible to obtain precise failure probabilities by mapping the quench dynamics in the quantum annealing window, which provides a crucial insight for implementing successful quantum annealing. By accounting for the effects of electron screening from the oxygen atoms, we found that it strengthens the tendency for this material to exhibit an antiferromagnetic phase and diminishes the likelihood of an unconventional superconducting state emerging. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the screening of the $d_{\perp}$ band by the $d_{\sigma}$ band plays a crucial role in understanding the absence of superconductivity in this material. Universal relations for stellar remnants, specifically relating the radius and mass of compact stars to their binding energy and pressure at the surface, have been identified as powerful tools for extracting their internal properties. However, these relations might not be universally applicable if compact stars with different masses exhibit distinct properties, such as strange quark matter behavior. We investigated the possibility of this scenario and examined the sound speed in dense stellar matter with strangeness using three models: the nonlinear sigma model with a $\sigma\omega\rho$-meson field, modified to include the $\kappa$-meson field, and a two-flavor quark-diquark model. In the first model, we determined the sound speed near the surface and at high densities, and found that it approaches its upper limit, approximately equal to 1, in the high-density regime. In the second model, we computed the sound speed within the core of quark stars and found that it ranges from 0.62 to 0.67, and that it could be as high as 0.7 for the most massive stars. In the third model, we calculated the sound speed within the core and found that it ranges from 0.4 to 0.5, and that it exhibits a mild dependence on mass. Generally, the sound speed in dense matter with strangeness is expected to be greater than 0.4, and less than 1, across various models. This research was conducted to accompany our previous study on universal relations, and to provide a framework for interpreting equations of state in dense matter with strangeness. Additionally, we extracted the sound speed at the core of compact stars with canonical masses, and found that it ranges from 0.46 to 0.67, and that it exhibits a weak dependence on mass, with a mean and standard deviation of $0.56\pm 0.06$. This prediction can be verified through astrophysical observations of compact stars, and may have implications for their possible existence with masses above 2 solar masses. This research also highlights the relationship between the sound speed and density of compact stars, and may have consequences for their quark matter equations of state, and therefore for their possible strange matter configurations. This in turn may have implications for the possibility of their existence with masses above 2 solar masses, and may be tested through their gravitational wave signatures, particularly in high-mass binary mergers. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a analytical and numerical study of dust development's impact on the VSI. Our findings indicate that particle growth may not significantly impact the VSI's development but does reduce its peak amplitude. Furthermore, larger particles settle at the disk's lower regions, potentially reducing VSI activity. In a model depicting an 0.01 to 10 AU wide disk, VSI activity is diminished by 20% at its innermost portion (0.1 to 3.2 AU) and more significantly (50%) further out (3.2 to 10 AU) as dust grows and settles. These outcomes suggest the VSI could be a less frequent phenomenon than previously thought, and its absence might still allow for particle settlement. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate vast amounts of text for answering, but this approach can result in performance issues due to the enormous amount of input data. In this paper, a two-step method is presented to manage large amounts of text on the fly, allowing for more efficient question answering. First, a preliminary answer is obtained from a compact semantic graph, and then the response is refined using a trainer that incorporates additional relevant information. The proposed strategy is tested using the CommonsenseQA dataset and VCR, a recently introduced dataset that combines readingcomprehension with explicit commonsense verification. The results show that the proposed approach outperforms the baseline in question answering accuracy while successfully managing large amounts of input data. The code for the proposed approach is available at https://github.com/ghru/Co2C.

Individuals within the criminal justice system are undergoing a significant transformation, as many states are mandating mental health treatment for those they convict. This study examines a novel requirement introduced in 2011 by the Michigan 72nd District Court, which made mental health treatment compulsory for a subset of convicted offenders. We compared the mental health and well-being of individuals subject to this new rule with those not affected by it, utilizing a sample of over 1,500 defendants from the same district court obtained through a survey conducted in 2019. The data shows that, for the most part, required treatment had a positive impact on the mental health of offenders who had easy access to the program, with particular benefits seen in those with severe mental health issues, suicidal tendencies, or substance abuse problems. However, we found that some offenders experienced negative outcomes, with 13% reporting decreased motivation and 11% stating it led to strained relationships with family and friends. Offenders who struggled with access to the program or felt coerced into it by the court order tended to have more adverse reactions. The study highlights the complexities surrounding court-ordered mental health treatment and highlights policy implications to consider, including the importance of accessible programs and obtaining the consent of those required to participate. The findings suggest that a one-size-fits-all approach to mental health treatment within the criminal justice system may not be effective and that a more nuanced strategy is necessary to achieve positive outcomes. The research also underlines the value of survey data obtained from court samples and provides a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of various justice system interventions. The case of Michigan offers valuable policy lessons for other jurisdictions considering similar required treatment programs. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper addresses that challenge by introducing a new regularization technique, consistent regularization via reconstruction. This technique utilizes an unsupervised, automatically learned image representation that complements the limited annotated data. By leveraging this representation in a consistent manner, it achieves a balance between oversmoothing the annotated regions and preserving unseen information. The proposed method is straightforward to implement and incorporates consistent regularization via reconstruction directly into the loss function using a simple and efficient technique. Our research showcases the effectiveness of consistent regularization via reconstruction for semi-supervised medical image segmentation tasks. We tested this method against three widely used benchmarks and observed significant improvements in segmentation accuracy with simple implementation requirements. The proposed technique has a direct applicability to other semi-supervised image segmentation tasks beyond medical imaging. In 1963, Feynman hypothesized that a complex quantum system's dynamics could be understood and predicted based on the behavior of its individual components, without referencing the overall system. This idea has been successfully applied to various scenarios, but for extremely intricate and interconnected systems, this approach has proven unfruitful. To address this challenge, our research introduces a novel methodology that combines a graph neural network with a quantum-inspired training mechanism, allowing for a precise analysis of a system's energy levels. By leveraging a range of approximation techniques, this framework also provides insights into a system's temporal dynamics and identifies the influence of individual atoms on the overall chaos it exhibits. To validate our approach, we utilized a realistic superconducting circuit model comprising 4, 5, and 6 coupled qubits, and demonstrated that even with a relatively unrefined approximation, our methodology accurately predicts the coherence times and energy spectra of these systems. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the distinct contributions of each qubit to the system's chaos, revealing critical insights that have been previously unaccessible. In the realm of open systems, our research has also discovered that the interaction with the environment can sometimes result in a re-emergence of coherence, a phenomenon that has been visually captured in a time-domain diagram. We aim to determine the optimal estimator for the parameter of interest, under a certain mixing distribution, using a generalized maximum likelihood estimation framework. Our primary contribution establishes that, when the set of possible mixing distributions is specified, the average parameter under a unknown mixing distribution can be estimated through a weighted maximum likelihood estimation procedure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this estimator is asymptotically efficient and gauge the distance between the proposed estimator and the ideal target parameter, under a specific mixing distribution. Our analysis encompasses a broad range of scenarios, from finite sets of possible mixing distributions to regular families of mixing distributions, and even scenarios in which the set of possible mixing distributions is specified as the set of all probability measures on a compact space. Our results also yield insights into the asymptotic behavior of the proposed estimator when the set of possible mixing distributions is not restricted, and we show that our estimator is analogous to the conventional maximum likelihood estimator used in sampling scenarios, such as capture-recapture experiments or mixture models. Knowledge Tracing (KT) models leverage student interaction data to predict upcoming correct answers, and their effectiveness is typically assessed using proctored online assessments as ground truth. However, utilizing full proctored assessments for model evaluation and training can be impractical due to their extensive nature. Thus, a more feasible method involves utilizing partially proctored assessments, which have been observed and marked for completeness. Presently, research on KT models primarily focuses on validation, without consideration for missing marked answers. As a result, current evaluation metrics do not accurately account for the degree of completeness in partially proctored assessments. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a novel approach for evaluating KT models, which takes into consideration the marked and unanswered questions in partially proctored assessments. This evaluation method rewards models for correctly forecasting unmarked answers among numerous possible unmarked answers. We have developed a Python library called pyKT to implement this evaluation method, which allows for exploration of different evaluation metrics, unmarked answer prediction, as well as analysis of model performance across partially proctored assessments. We have further conducted an experiment to demonstrate the usefulness of our evaluation method and associated library. In this experiment, we evaluated a state-of-the-art KT model using assessments from the Learning Analytics Campaign (LAC) dataset, and our results showed that KT models can be improved by simply using our evaluation method. We have made the Python library pyKT available to the public, in the hope that it will be beneficial to the research community. Ten years ago, at the inaugural Symla workshop, full first-class expressions in SMT solvers were a novel concept, with solvers like CVC3 and SMT06 offering a new level of flexibility through explicit terms within their logic. Since then, this idea has become a standard in SMT solving, with solvers like Z3, CVC4, and VeriT incorporating full first-class expressions into their designs. Building upon this foundation, the next logical step is to make arguments to these solvers also first-class, enabling the solvers to manipulate proofs in a more flexible manner. We present Alethe, a language designed to create and manipulate arguments that can be used with SMT solvers featuring full first-class logic. We demonstrate the practical applications of Alethe by integrating it with the Z3 solver, resulting in a system that can both verify the validity of arguments and, in addition, make available the original proof that led to those arguments, in a purified form of the Z3 theory. We also provide empirical evidence of the performance of this integrated system on a diverse set of verification proofs generated from real-world projects. Lastly, we outline potential future extensions to Alethe, and the benefits they could provide to a broader community of users, including developers of verification tools and the Z3 solver in particular. In its current and anticipated forms, Alethe offers a novel and valuable tool with widespread uses, as it enables the transparent handling of doubts raised against the validity of certain project verifications. In the process of creating this document, we encountered several challenges that could have prevented us from fully exploring all possible features of Alethe, especially with regard to its interaction with solvers that have a more complex design than the Z3 solver. Nevertheless, we are confident that our current implementation and the approaches we used to solve the encountered challenges could serve as a foundation for similar projects aimed at creating more intricate proofs formats, as well as providing a practical solution for our specific use case. The source code of Alethe is available at https://github.com/alethe-language/alethe. The integrated system based on Z3 is available at https://github.com/alethe-language/alethe-z3. We present both systems as part of the Alethe project on GitHub, in addition to the documents containing the challenges we faced and the ways we overcame them, as well as the guidelines we used to create the language and the resulting system. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates, where devices send graded updates to the server at their own pace without waiting for previous communications. In order to accommodate asynchronous updates, FedBuff employs a buffered aggregation method that considers the rates at which devices submit updates. This algorithm allows for efficient learning across diverse datasets with significantly different sample sizes. Our experimental results on synthetic data and real-world datasets, in particular MNIST and Shuffled Census Data, demonstrate that FedBuff achieves comparable performance to synchronized learning, and significantly outperforms the base federated learning model. In particular, FedBuff shows a 12.7% reduction in the gap between centralized learning and federated learning on real-world data. Our findings also highlight the importance of proper scheduling and data heterogeneity. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghraiesi/UnrestrictedGradients.

By utilizing Gaussian Process regression, our method generates a compact dataset of optimal actions for the robot to follow, even with a limited number of observations.  We introduce a new sparse TD learning model that leverages this reduced dataset and incorporates the concept of action values, resulting in a new sparse TD learning model.  We also develop an approximate solution to the non-sparse version of the model and establish the convergence rate of its natural policy iteration algorithm.  Through careful simulation studies, our results demonstrate that the natural policy iteration algorithm outperforms the standard TD learning method, particularly in highly dynamic environments.  We also test the model on a real underwater robot platform and observe a significant improvement in its performance.  Our approach can be applied to a broad range of TD learning problems involving partially observable environments.  We conclude by discussing some unaddressed research questions, including the development of an online variant of the model and its application to problems involving delayed rewards feedback.  We also provide a detailed derivation of the natural policy iteration algorithm's convergence rate. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper leverages the framework of meta-learning to enable efficient domain adaptation for GEC without relying on pseudo data. A novel approach is proposed involving two stages: a initial submission of raw translations, followed by human evaluation and refinement. In the few-shot transfer stage, the model is fine-tuned for a curated dataset of high-quality translations in the target domain. Evaluation on the NCON test set shows significant gains in METEOR scores for domains with 200-500 example sentences available, and notable improvements in other metrics for domains with 500-2000 example sentences. Additionally, the proposed method demonstrates high quality translations in the FLORE dataset with an average of 3.3 human evaluation points out of 5.00. Code available at: https://github.com/PRASENJIT/FewShotGEC.git. Human annotations used in this work are available at: https://github.com/PRASENJIT/FewShotGEC.git#macaw.

In a scenario where multiple agents compete for limited, high-value goods without the ability to make side deals, we are interested in examining the efficiency and fairness of two prominent mechanisms: the Vickrey-Clarke-Roughgarden-Mehran (VCRM) mechanism and the proportional mechanism. Specifically, we focus on pure-Nash equilibria, a more robust form of stability. Our primary goals are to assess the efficacy of these mechanisms in both individual and competitive settings. Individually, both mechanisms yield desirable outcomes, albeit the VCRM mechanism offers greater efficiency with no sacrifice of fairness, as it guarantees the highest possible utility for each agent. In a competitive setting, the VCRM mechanism maintains its fairness properties while ensuring that each agent values the goods at least as highly as they cost. The proportional mechanism, on the other hand, is more fragile, as it relies on agents' perceptions of others' values. In a competitive context, this mechanism's fairness guarantees are limited, and it may result in outcomes that are less efficient than optimal. Notably, the proportionality mechanism has a critical issue with fairness, as it may prioritize the interests of higher-valued goods over benefit, potentially leading to outcomes that are essentially random in regards to distributional fairness. In a competitive context, the VCRM mechanism can offer a significant advantage over the proportionality mechanism in terms of distributive fairness, achieving the "right" outcome in a wide range of value spaces. In both individual and competitive settings, we identify specific values that yield outcomes that are fair, efficient, and optimal. Our analysis also involves an explicit characterization of the set of pure-Nash equilibria induced by the VCRM mechanism and the proportionality mechanism, as well as an exploration of how the quality of these equilibria compares to optimal outcomes, particularly with regard to efficiency and distributive fairness. Finally, we provide a lower bound on the gap between the utility an agent can obtain in a pure-Nash equilibrium induced by the VCRM mechanism and the maximum possible utility, which we find to be directly proportional to the largest good's value and the square of the number of goods. Our current best knowledge involves a specific instance in which the proportionality mechanism's fairness guarantee fails entirely, leading to an outcome that is fundamentally unfair. Our results were obtained using a combination of our own analytical methods, as well as results from recent studies on the VCRM mechanism's stability and the complexity of pure-Nash equilibria induced by mechanisms. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. The anomalous distribution of its star formation also makes UGC 8839 a prime subject for further study of the interplay between galaxy interactions, the stability of galaxy disks, and the conversion of gas to stars. The extensive data available for UGC 8839, including high-resolution Hubble Space Telescope imagery, facilitate a range of derivative analyses, including the construction of a detailed three-dimensional model of its disk, the calculation of its total mass, and the observation of stellar tidal streams on either side of the galaxy indicating that it has undergone a close approach to a massive companion galaxy in the recent past. The unique characteristics of UGC 8839 also make it an intriguing subject for further study of the distribution and behavior of its globular cluster population, the abundance patterns of its stellar populations, and the overall chemical composition of the galaxy. The extensive data available for UGC 8839 can be accessed through a range of online resources, including the Hubble Space Telescope Archive, the HyperCatalog of NASA's SkyMap, the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, the GALEX Multi-Wave Length Survey, the IRAS Faint Images of the Sky, the 2MASS All-Sky Catalog, and the All-Sky Automated Survey for SuperNovae. The various analyses conducted of UGC 8839 highlight the value of combining observational data from a range of sources, the importance of using appropriate scaling factors when analyzing the distribution of its star formation, and the prevalence of HII regions at greater galactocentric radii in low-mass spiral galaxies. Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of hadron structure is conducted by calculating distribution functions that identify the origin of quarks and gluons within a pion. A novel method is employed which compares the distribution of a quark's charge within the piron on the one hand, and the distribution of quark and gluon charges on the other. Calculating these distributions for various currents, both with and without two-current associations, provides insight into the pion's charge distribution. A comparison is made between distributions derived from three types of quark currents: axial, vector, and scalar. Although the overall charge distributions appear similar, differences arise when examining two-current associations in detail. For example, the proportion of charge attributed to the association of a quark with a quark or a quark with a gluon changes depending on the current used. These results highlight the complexity of hadron distribution functions and the importance of two-current associations non-trivially, effectively counter to naive interpretations of the Balitsky-Friman-Kroll (BFK) approximation. Moreover, disagreements with the BFK approximation are observed, particularly when examining the distribution of a quark's charge within the pion. Furthermore, a distinction is drawn between the distribution of a quark's charge and the distribution of quark and gluon charges, demonstrating that two-current associations are necessary to accurately describe hadron distribution functions. These findings suggest that hadron distribution functions should not be interpreted without considering two-current associations, and that such associations are a fundamental aspect of hadron structure that requires further investigation. A comparison is also made between these results and the outcomes of perturbative QCD calculations. These outcomes disagree with the outcomes of lattice calculations, with perturbative calculations overestimating the proportion of charge attributed to the association of a quark with a gluon. These discrepancies could be a consequence of the origins of hadron distribution functions being non-perturbative, as indicated by the outcomes of lattice calculations. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
robust and scalable systems involving multiple interacting entities.
However, offline multi-agent reinforcement learning is challenging due to the
variability of observed interactions.
This research introduces a novel approach, focused on offline learning for
two-agent interactive tasks, where the objective is distinct from many
standard scenarios.
Rather than prioritizing cooperative outcomes, we emphasize the significance
of learning from high-quality individual experiences, given the prevalence of
selfish behavior in many situations.
Key contribution includes a tailored method that leverages both positive
and negative experiences, and a meaningful evaluation setup that mimics real
world interactions.
Overall, our work demonstrates tangible improvements in performance when
learning from mixed data sets, incorporating both positive and negative
experiences. 
We also explore the connection between our method and existing techniques,
as well as the impact of our approach under varying degree of cooperation. 
Finally, we address limitations and potential avenues for further
development.

The alignment of megavoltage images is a critical step in radiation therapy, enabling the accurate localization of tumors across different image modalities. Our research involves training a convolutional neural network to align 2D/3D images obtained through megavoltage imaging, with particular focus on aligning images taken before and during treatment. To evaluate the network's performance, we compared it with a registered ground truth using normalized mutual information (NMI) and mean squared error (MSE) metrics. The results showed that the NMI score averaged 0.93 across 20 randomly selected image pairs, while the network's performance in relation to ground truth was also reflected in a low MSE value of 3.02610^-3. Our analysis of treatment monitoring images revealed that the network effectively handled cases with low tumor changes, averaging an NMI score of 0.88. Moreover, by incorporating a dropout technique, we found that the network's performance could be improved, with a corresponding increase in training time. The proposed network's simplicity allows it to be trained on a regular PC, whereas more complex setups are required for more advanced models. V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly three and a half days while the absence of the white dwarf spin frequency presents further evidence for a massive WD.  The pre and post nova energy distributions also indicate a massive accretion rate.  V392 Persei, unlike many novae and dwarf novae systems, did not switch to its initial low mass transfer configuration, but instead stayed in its high mass transfer state, which we believe is as a result of the irradiation of the companion by the massive nova explosion, thus it exhibits a level of similarity with another renowned system known as GK Persei.  The extensive electron capture of 12C by 1H, which is an unusual nova reaction, is also reflected in both the initial and ongoing spectra of V392 Persei, which has never been observed in any other nova.  The nova also reflects unique insights regarding the distribution, the optical thickness of the ejected particles as well as the extent of the illuminated accretion disk.  V392 Persei, which reflects an extraordinary level of insight regarding the internal dynamics of novae as well as the reactions that take place within them, presents a level of sustained activity that challenges the long held belief that classic novae are transient objects.  The extensive duration of its eruption, combined with the level of insight it has provided regarding its inner workings, make it an object that astronomers will be studying for years to come.  V392 Persei, which declined to a level of luminosity similar to that of its pre nova levels over nearly three years, exhibited persistent levels of luminosity as well as heat and light that was being generated through the interaction between the mass that had been ejected during its eruption and the accretion disk that was still being fed by its companion. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to create a codebook and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our enhanced version, we conducted a series of comparisons with the original untuned TextWorld levels, showing that our optimized version delivers comparable results while significantly reducing runtime. 
Our findings also highlight a notable discrepancy between the time it takes agent-based learning systems to complete each level in the original and our optimized versions, emphasizing the critical role of speed in text-based gaming competitions.

Our research underscores the significance of considering speed as a key factor in evaluating and comparing text-based gaming challenges and platforms. 
We believe that TextWorldExpress serves as a model for future best practices in creating and optimizing complex simulations.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in neuroscience research, and Bayes factors have gained popularity for this purpose. We explore various workflow approaches in neuroscience research utilizing Bayes factors, examining how results are currently being employed. Our study investigates the types of analyses conducted, the frequency of reproducibility demands, and the methods used to interpret Bayes factors. We discovered that the majority of studies apply a straightforward approach, assessing whether the posterior probability of a hypothesis exceeds a certain threshold, often without considering the issues related to this methodical approach, such as prior influence and the need for replication. We highlight potential pitfalls and alternatives for these approaches, emphasizing the value of Bayesian model comparison for evaluating models, the utilization of bridge sampling for computing Bayes factors, and the use of bayes factor distribution to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the evidence. We also provide free access to our previously developed Python toolbox, BayesFactor. With this paper, we aim to promote more rigorous methods for evaluating hypotheses and interpreting Bayes factors, encouraging our peers to engage in a more critical assessment of neuroscience research. We welcome feedback on our workshop approach, our code, and our methods, hoping this exchange will contribute to the advancement of hypothesis evaluation in neuroscience. Specifically, we consider the case where a matrix $X$ is partitioned into $A$ sub-matrices, and we aim to minimize the function $f(X) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^A C_i \log(X^{-1} \Omega_i X^{-1})$ subject to the matrix $X$ being positive definite. Here, $\Omega_i$ are given matrices, and $C_i$ are positive scalar weights. We establish that the matrix optimization problem has a geodesically convex domain when the positive definite matrix manifold is equipped with a particular Riemannian metric induced by the Euclidean metric defined on the space of symmetric matrices. This geodesic convexity is demonstrated to hold true for a specific choice of weights $C_i$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the problem can be reformulated as a geodesically convex minimization problem on a manifold of matrices with a particular rank, and this is our main contribution. Lastly, this formulation enables us to leverage the monitoring role of the Riemannian gradient, which is an aspect that is distinct from the approach adopted in our recent work. The proposed strategy is further compared against other state-of-the-art algorithms, and our results show that our proposed strategy is consistently superior to other comparison methods. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. After exploring existing methods to mitigate faults within CNNs, including technique combinations and optimized max-pooling, we focus on activation range supervision (ARS) as a means of enhancing resilience. By limiting input images to a defined color range, ARS stabilizes CNNs and minimizes the risk of faulty memory influencing deployment outcomes. Furthermore, we establish guidelines for deriving suitable color ranges through simple, non-technical means, making it an accessible solution for various real-world applications. Despite its simplicity, ARS is shown to provide robust performance comparable to more sophisticated fault tolerance techniques, demonstrating the efficacy of a conservative, initial approach to creating a safety case for vision-based systems used in critical contexts. To facilitate widespread adoption, we make our ARS code available to the public.

In late October 2019, violent demonstrations and widespread unrest gripped Chile, primarily targeting the country's capital, Santiago. To model this phenomenon, we employ an epidemiological approach, extending an earlier framework that accounted for symptoms' manifestation delay and described the spread of disease within a localized community. The original method assumed that infected individuals remain asymptomatic for a week before displaying symptoms and suggested that approximately 7 days would elapse before the peak number of new infections occurs. However, this model fell short of accurately capturing the pattern observed in Santiago, where the primary area of outbreak showed a more pronounced time lag of over a week, likely resulting from greater social distancing measures in place from the outset. To better explain this discrepancy, we introduce a new variation of the model, incorporating the concept of distinct levels of infection prevalence in more and less populated areas and incorporating a longer asymptomatic period of 10 days in the former. The resulting simulation reproduces the observed delay and reflects the unique characteristics of Santiago's population, also implying that the initial asymptomatic period could be a critical factor influencing the pace of an epidemic's progression. Furthermore, this variation enables control measures such as increased asymptomatic period duration to be identified as key factors in themselves, rather than an inevitable consequence of a longer pre-symptomatic period. The model's flexibility also allows it to be applied to other scenarios, such as modeling the spread of the disease across different geographic regions with varying population densities. Mobile agents require accurate localization, and while VIO can perform well, it struggles with low-frame-rate inertial measurements and significant occlusions. This paper introduces EMA-VIO, a deep visual-inertial localization method that employs an external memory attention mechanism to effectively combine the measurements from an inertial measurement unit. In addition to using the external memory, a state regression module and a measurement correction module are used to correct the measurements and estimate the state. Unlike current methods that use a deterministic state and measurement update, our approach uses a distributional state prediction that provides uncertainty. This uncertainty is utilized in a Gaussian weighting function in the external memory, enabling the selection of relevant inertial data. We further introduce a patch-based attention mechanism to enable the agent to explore a larger environment by locally weighting the inertial data based on the mapping. We demonstrate the effectiveness of EMA-VIO on two datasets, where it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of localization accuracy and reduces the reliance on the inertial measurements during intense occlusions. The code has been made available at: https://github.com/liyeyan/EMA-VIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, yet certain materials exhibit non-linear responses that could influence quantum measurements. A specific class of materials, known as topological Weyl materials, exhibit non-linear response characteristics and feature three-fold degeneracy at certain points in their structure. These materials have no low-energy states near their band gaps, which makes their non-linear response solely of extrinsic origin. In this study, we introduce a new class of materials, dubbed square-root higher-order Weyl materials, which have no low-energy states near their band gaps and exhibit non-linear response characteristics of both intrinsic and extrinsic origins. Unlike standard WeyL materials, they have a four-fold degeneracy at certain points in their structure. A key feature of these materials is that their non-linear response characteristics can be influenced by both the intrinsic properties and the boundary conditions. We investigate the possible points of degeneracy and the associated topological charges in square-root higher-order Weyl materials, and demonstrate that their non-linear response characteristics are influenced by the intrinsic properties and the boundary conditions. We also propose an all-in-orbiton scenario of square-root higher-order Weyl materials, and demonstrate that it exhibits both the four-fold degeneracy and the all-in-orbiton phenomenon. We further investigate the impact of square-root higher-order Weyl materials on light and matter waves, and demonstrate that it leads to non-linear interactions between the materials and their surroundings. This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. The study indicates that the proposed scheme yields accurate and smooth reconstructions, even in the presence of gated boundaries or with inaccurate or missing boundary data. The approach can be applied to other similar inversion problems involving elliptic equations and provides a starting point for exploring more complex time-dependent problems. In the context of advancing AI through numerous data sources with limited collaborations, knowledge amalgamation emerges as a vital technique. This process integrates diverse knowledge bases with different representation formats by matching their contents. However, developing practical and scalable methods to merge knowledge bases efficiently remains a significant challenge. Our innovation addresses this issue by introducing the first method to integrate four different knowledge bases in a federated setting. This approach achieves integration through a two-step process: initially matching content, and subsequently selecting relevant data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by pairing four diverse knowledge bases, including text-based Wikipedia and spreadsheet-based Cytoscape. The results show that our approach outperforms existing methods in various evaluation metrics, surpassing the state-of-the-art in both content matching and data selection tasks. Moreover, our method excels in a real-world scenario, integrating four knowledge bases around the COVID-19 topic. Our solution is available as an open-source tool on GitHub, primed for problem-solving in various knowledge amalgamation scenarios. In a notable demonstration, we integrated over 100 Wikipedia articles across four different bases. The results of our experiments highlight the scalability and efficiency of our method, yielding a 94% precision rate in content matching and a 86% coverage rate in data selection. In a further innovation, we expand our approach to handle incomplete knowledge bases, a critical aspect often overlooked in existing research. In a real-world application, we integrated Wikipedia knowledge bases with incomplete spreadsheets, obtaining a 75% coverage rate in content matching and a 60% precision rate in data selection. In a notable variation, we explored a simpler version of our method, reducing the complexity of content matching by limiting spreadsheet searches to specific columns. The results showed that this variant excels in spreading data selection over multiple columns, achieving a 30% better performance compared to the standard approach. In a further expansion, we expand our method to handle multiple spreadsheet data sources, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in combining three different spreadsheets with diverse formats, achieving a 25% better performance in content matching and a 20% better performance in data selection compared to the standard approach. We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves in quartic extensions of the rationals, focusing on cases where the quartic field has a Galois extension with the symmetric group $S_4$ or $A_4$. Using methods from arithmetic geometry and particularly Kummer theory, we examine how the rank of an elliptic curve changes under these conditions. It is shown that within $S_4$ extensions, there are infinitely many instances where the rank of an elliptic curve increases, given certain initial rank conditions. On the other hand, we also establish the existence of infinitely many $A_4$ extensions where the rank of an elliptic curve does not change, provided a specific conjecture is true. Additionally, we provide explicit examples of both types. It is worth noting that our results rely on the conjectural Mertens' conjecture and a result from a previous study by Goldfeld and Tamagnini. Furthermore, our findings related to $S_4$ extensions generalize results from a prior study by Goldfeld and Tamagnini, whereas our $A_4$-related results generalize a prior result from a study by Elkies and Goldfeld. Both types of results can be found in a broader context within a recent study by Gross and Zagier. Lastly, it is also possible to modify our results to investigate the rank growth of elliptic curves in other number fields with a similar structure.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. Additionally, we analyze the impact of substrate choice and carrier concentration on resonator decay rates and quantum volume. This research highlights the significance of terahertz investigations in evaluating and developing quantum devices, and provides experimental evidence for a previously hypothesized decay pathway induced by silicon erosion. Moreover, we explore various silicon etching techniques to optimize carrier concentrations, reducing the overlap between the microwave field and silicon areas with high carrier concentrations. This study focuses on basic resonators, but also examines coupled junctions, a crucial element for quantum computing, and investigates the etching of a single junction to increase the quantum volume. We estimate the potential increase in coherence time to be approximately one order of magnitude, based on theoretical simulations. This study paves the way for investigating and evaluating other quantum devices, such as Josephson parametric amplifiers, upon the underlying materials. This includes analyzing the terahertz properties of materials, investigating the etching techniques, and evaluating the influence of carrier concentrations and etching patterns on the performance of quantum devices. This research was conducted at the terahertz near-field microscopy facility at Chalmers University, Sweden. A key aspect of exoplanetary science is understanding how atmospheres of varying composition maintain their current state through the balance of internal and external factors including solar radiation, geological activity, and temperature. To that end, a focus on the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere is crucial as well as the potential pathways its atmosphere may have followed in the distant past. In a recent workshop, researchers delved into the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere and explored the various processes that have shaped its composition over time, also examining the potential mechanisms that may have influenced its past state, with results presented in a proceedings paper. A notable finding from the meeting's discussion was the significance of atmospheric oscillations in responding to changes in solar energy and geological activity, with consequences for the atmosphere's stability being influenced by various feedback loops involving cloud cover, albedo, and temperature. These interactions can cause the atmosphere to exhibit behavior at equilibrium rather than a linear response to external factors. In examining the historical development of Venus's atmosphere, several scenarios emerged including turbulent early conditions, massive resurfacing events, and various periods of volcanic activity, all with distinct implications for the planet's present state, with some leading to atmospheric retention or loss, and even instances of snowball or runaway hothouse states. In studying these possibilities, researchers found several potential indicators of past geological activity including the surface age, volcanic flux, and surface heat budget, with estimates suggesting activity ceased anywhere from 500 million to 1 billion years ago, although some believe activity may have stopped even earlier, with consequences for the atmosphere's current state, with scenarios ranging from stable to unstable conditions. In analyzing the potential for atmospheric escape, researchers found that the rate of escape is influenced by solar wind, magnetic field strength, and atmospheric composition, with outcomes including stable to unstable conditions, and even instances of massive escape leading to a retained or lost atmosphere. In examining the interactions between the atmosphere, geology, and solar influences, researchers found several critical pointers, with consequences for exoplanetary research, and a need for further investigation into key areas including atmospheric retention and loss, magnetic field strength, and solar influences, with results from the meeting presented in 13 individual papers.

As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component, which the research demonstrates functions efficiently with terawatt laser powers, alters the polarization of laser pulses while increasing their intensity by several times, and this effect can be controlled by adjusting the magnetic field strength. Furthermore, simulations show that this component can effectively convert circularly polarized light into linearly polarized light within a wide range of laser wavelengths, including those employed in petawatt-range laser systems. This novel waveplate offers a promising means of overcoming the limitations of solid-state optics and provides a versatile tool for an array of high-power laser applications. The effectiveness of X-ray monitoring at intermediate sensitivity is reliant on wide-field optical monitors that can rapidly move between different sky configurations. However, the limited number of suitable telescopes capable of meeting these requirements highlights the significance of repurposing existing astronomical assets. We examine the potential for a segment of X-ray telescopes known as lobster-eye optics to be combined within a single system and explore the optical design's advantages and possible configurations. By joining four X-ray telescopes, we found that such a combined system could identify 50th magnitude supernovae within a few nights across a sky area of 10,000 square degrees, and with existing instruments readily available, this concept presents a feasible solution for medium-scale supernova surveys and other astronomical applications. Although our analysis centers on the Kueven lobster-eye design, this study's approach is adaptable to other similar configurations. The integrated system's efficacy is highly dependent on the individual components and their interactions, meaning that a detailed, customized analysis is necessary to optimize its performance for a specific astronomical target. The challenge of tracking and aligning the telescopes' positions in real-time may be addressed using various technologies, including optical, mechanical, and software-based methods. These controls allow for the modification of an initial state's boundary, and the problem's value function is found to be harmonic with respect to a modified distance function. These findings are then used to derive upper and lower bounds for the control problem's value function. These results extend and improve previous work, and demonstrate the utility of level set methods in solving partial uniform ellipticity problems. The paper also discusses the relationship between partial uniform ellipticity and a specific class of a priori estimates that are crucial for its solution. These estimates involve the solution to a nonlinear stochastic HJB equation, and are demonstrated to be equivalent to the solution's boundedness for an appropriate class of initial data. These results are then used to analyse the solution's behaviour as the distance between the initial data and the set where the control is defined increases. To investigate the impact of cosmic velocity field on dark matter halo mass function, we employed a deep learning approach with a generative adversarial network. To accommodate the variable velocity field, we developed a new method of sample synthesis through noise injection in the generator, allowing for the production of training sets with diverse velocity characteristics analogous to those observed in the actual universe. These generated samples replicated the relationships between velocity, density, and bias found in observed data and proved effective in validating fundamental assumptions of traditional halo mass function models. Furthermore, we utilized these generated samples to examine the influence of velocity field on halo mass function, discovering a direct relationship between the standard deviation of velocity field and the shift of the mean density threshold. This resulted in an expression for velocity's impact on the halo mass function and enabled a computational validation of our findings using an existing simulation. The learned features from our model also granted insight into the underlying assumptions of traditional models, and its efficiency in generating samples was found to surpass conventional methods by an order of magnitude. Ultimately, our analysis demonstrated a simple yet conclusive answer to the question of how the velocity field affects the halo mass function, and our results are applicable to low and high velocity regimes alike. The developed model's capability in replicating observations and simulations makes it a valuable analytical tool, and our findings are relevant to ongoing and future large-scale structure surveys such as LOFAR, SIMON, and SKA. The model's efficacy in generating samples at various scales and in different velocity regimes opens up possibilities for further investigations into the relationships between velocity, bias, and density, including the analysis of individual components of the velocity field and its effect on the halo mass function along different axes. The model's scalability to higher resolution and larger range of velocity spectra at the expense of accuracy remains a subject of interest for ongoing and future research.
