We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. These simulations resulted in a range of outcomes, from subtle changes in initial equilibrium configurations to more dramatic events like core collapse and massive star formation. 

Our research began with the fundamental principles of general relativity and Lagrangian formulation, and we have developed a novel numerical technique called the "semi-lagrangian" method, which has given us insights into both static and dynamic configurations in rotating stars. This method has also allowed us to introduce small perturbations or fluctuations in equilibrium configurations, which could be useful in modeling real stars and their behavior. 

Among the many applications of our method is the simulation of massive star formation, which could help us understand how massive stars are formed and their key characteristics, and has also led to the discovery of previously unknown ways that low-mass stars can form and influence their surroundings. Our research has further revealed that even low-mass stars can experience massive mergers and the resulting outcomes, and has paved the way for a new generation of realistic simulations of star and galaxy formation. 

Our code is highly efficient, scalable, and flexible, and has been designed to utilize advanced computational resources, which has allowed us to simulate complex phenomena on an unprecedented scale, and has further enabled us to integrate our code with other codes, which has given us insights into a wide range of phenomena, from the formation of individual stars to the behavior of entire galaxies.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. In fact, our results indicate that, depending on the specific dataset in question, this method can even lead to models with a higher overall accuracy compared to traditional labeling methods. Our approach has the added benefit of making it much more practical to create custom models tailored to a particular document type, given the ease with which new models can be trained on the basis of a single annotated document. Our code is available at GitHub at the following location: https://github.com/google/selected-awareness. Our proposed approach opens the door to applying state-of-the-art document extraction models in a wide range of contexts, where it has so far been difficult to acquire enough high-quality labeled data. This is achievable thanks to the extremely low data labeling costs involved, which in our experiments were found to be as little as $0.01 per document. This is a particularly significant development given the high costs traditionally associated with labeling documents. Our proposed approach was awarded the best paper award at the ACL 2023 conference. Our proposed approach can be applied to a wide range of tasks that involve analyzing and processing visually complex documents, in addition to extraction. This includes but is not limited to classification, classification with multiple classes, and ranking. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches achieve this by employing matched filters with sufficient precision but usually fail to account for signal uncertainties and uncertainties in neutron star dense matter. We introduce an alternative method based on deep learning, which employs a convolutional neural network to differentiate signals from noise and accurately classify signals from all possible neutron star binary combinations, even with a 10% uncertainty in dense matter state parameters. This method's efficacy is demonstrated through the successful real-time analysis of live gravitational wave data from the LIGO and Virgo detectors. Furthermore, we introduce an open-source, user-friendly Python package called $NeuWave$, which incorporates this deep learning model and facilitates easy integration into real-time analysis systems for a range of compact binary mergers. NeuWave is optimized for high-performance computing platforms and incorporates multi-threading technology to maximize computational efficiency. Consequently, this package offers an cost-effective and scalable solution for the rapid identification and classification of signals from compact binary mergers in real-time, and is suitable for use on a wide range of high-performance computing platforms, from large-scale supercomputers to modest desktop machines. We also explore NeuWave's capabilities on a range of compact binary mergers, including binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events, and analyze its performance on a range of dense matter state parameter combinations, including different neutron star equations of state, spin effects, and misalignment angles. Finally, we introduce an open dataset comprising 65000 simulated waveforms, available for electromagnetic radiation analysis and 20000 classified signals, available for training custom deep learning models. This research was conducted as part of the Grid Computational Infrastructure project.

Social distancing measures implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic significantly reduced urban encounters, leading to an decline in face-to-face social interactions outside of work or school settings. While overall encounter frequency fell, different socioeconomic groups responded to the pandemic in varying ways, with some reducing their external interactions more drastically than others. As a result, the divergence in social encounters among people of different incomes became more pronounced. A study analyzing encounters in the city of Ann Arbor, Michigan before and during the pandemic found that the middle class, which already had a narrower margin of income diversity, saw its encounters decrease more significantly than other income groups. Consequently, the middle class's income diversity diminished more during this period. It's essential to note that public transportation usage declined more rapidly than any individual income group's responses to the pandemic, which further contributed to a decline in urban encounters. Nonetheless, in Ann Arbor, public transportation usage accounted for a relatively small portion of the city's encounters. Notably, the pandemic's impact varied across different age groups, with younger individuals showing a greater decrease in encounters than older populations. Additionally, people with higher educational levels exhibited different behavior in responses to the pandemic, with Ph.D. holders reducing their encounters more than those with a bachelor's degree. Finally, the pandemic's effect on income diversity was more pronounced among certain ethnic groups, with the diversity of encounters among non-Hispanic whites declining more than among other ethnic groups. A better comprehension of how people's behavior changed during the pandemic is crucial for developing strategies to mitigate the negative consequences of social distancing measures on urban encounters and income diversity. A possible approach could involve targeting specific groups that reduced their external interactions more severely or promoting encounters within particular ethnic or age-based subpopulations. A further analysis of the data reveals that people with higher incomes reduced their encounters more at home, rather than in public places, than those with lower incomes, and explores the implications of this finding for policy interventions aimed at increasing income diversity in urban settings. A key challenge in responding to the pandemic lies in balancing measures that reduce the spread of the virus with those that promote economic and social activity, requiring an understanding of the interplay between individual behavior and the broader social consequences of those actions. A notable aspect of the pandemic's impact involves the rise of remote work and reduced commuting, which has led to increased dissatisfaction with daily life among younger individuals who spend more time at home. A possible long-term effect of the pandemic could be an increase in the diversity of encounters in these age groups, although this hypothesis needs further validation with additional data.

A massive star's complex formation history is reflected in its elemental abundance abnormalities.  To understand the processes influencing massive star formation and chemistry, this study examines the various scenarios that lead to unusual chemical patterns under different physical conditions, using a 1D hydrodynamic model of a massive protostar and surrounding environment.  Analyzing and calculating abundance ratios for different elements, the research reveals that: the presence of unusual iron and silicon abundance ratios in some massive young stellar objects could result from the rapid accumulation of material during a brief period of protostar formation; similar ratios in other objects may be produced by the high-speed mergers of two low-mass prestellar objects; and objects with unusual carbon and nitrogen abundance ratios might be formed through the mergers of objects with different chemical compositions, or by accumulated material that was exposed to high levels of ionizing radiation.  These possible scenarios highlight the varied formation paths of massive stars and the diverse environments they influence, and could be tested by combining observational data with models of star formation, chemistry, and radiation.  Additionally, the study's results have implications for the distribution of chemical abundance ratios in the surrounding molecular clouds, and the objects that form from them.  Given the short timescales and specific conditions required for unusual abundance ratios, this study also suggests that most massive stars form within a few tens of thousands of years, and that their formation is generally completed before the onset of massive outflows that influence the surrounding environment, unlike previously held assumptions.  Furthermore, the research highlights the importance of considering the three-dimensional structure and evolution of massive star-forming regions, and the effects of their outflows on the surrounding gases and materials, in analyzing the abundance ratios of elements in young massive stellar objects.  This is achieved by combining the analysis of abundance ratios with the spatial distribution of molecular gases and the structure of outflows, as illustrated by the case of the massive star-forming region AFGL 2591. The results obtained from the new equation are compared to the existing Hamiltonian Dysthe equation, with the finding that the existing equation lacks a key term related to the circulation. Additionally, the impact of the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation's parameters on the waves' behavior is visually presented in a set of graphs. Autonomous navigation in unfamiliar territories poses a significant challenge for mobile robots, citing issues like safety and efficiency. To tackle this problem, researchers have explored layered navigation control systems that balance risk and progress across different levels of the environment. While these methods have demonstrated promise, they often fall short in incorporating sensory feedback effectively. This paper presents a novel approach that integrates forward-looking sonar sensors with a layered navigation controller, enabling the system to account for the sonar's limited field of view and sensor noise. A key innovation is the introduction of a sonar-based danger zone that extends the system's awareness beyond the sonar's physical range, while also providing a means to assess the likelihood of obstacles within that zone. This approach leads to the development of an obstacle avoidance module that employs the sonar feedback to calculate the expected risk of collision and adjusts the system's risk layer accordingly. A key feature of this module is its ability to operate during high-priority decision-making phases, despite limited sonar data available. A further advancement is the integration of a path refinement phase that employs the sonar data to correct the navigation path, following the initial decision-making phase. A key aspect of this phase is its simple and efficient design, incorporating the sonar feedback into the risk assessment and layer update process. A crucial advantage of this approach is the resulting system's ability to operate efficiently, with minimal computational requirements. A key challenge in developing the system was addressing the trade-off between risk-taking and path refinement, given the limited sonar data available during high-priority decision-making phases. A novel solution to this problem was found by introducing a threshold value that determines the level of sonar data integration with the risk assessment and layer update process. A further complication arose from the system's tendency to become trapped in local minima due to the integrated sonar feedback and layered navigation controller. A key innovation in addressing this issue was the development of a pseudo-random number generator algorithm that disrupts the system's exploration of the environment and prevents it from becoming stuck in local minima. A novel aspect of this algorithm is its low computational cost and simplicity. A key feature of the pseudo-random number generator algorithm is its integration with the layered navigation controller, enabling the system to assess the risk of collision with unseen obstacles. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. Moreover, our findings highlight potential areas for improvement in the underlying architecture of large pre-trained language models, paving the way for future expansions in multiple applications. We also provide a dedicated code repository to facilitate replication and exploration of this research. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/ghulamabidkhan/CMTR-BERT. We further present a detailed analysis of the explicit biases present in BERT, demonstrating how its training data's inherent constraints limit its potential performance in specific tasks. This analysis is accompanied by a dedicated appendix available at https://github.com/ghulamabidkhan/CMTR-BERT-Appendix. We also examine the influence of varying summary lengths on our proposed text representation integration method, discovering that optimal performance is achieved at intermediate length thresholds, which we believe holds value for the broader community. We conclude by outlining potential future research avenues, including but not limited to, in-depth analyses of the biases present in BERT, and exploring our method's applicability to other tasks, such as question answering. We suggest several possible approaches for these avenues in the paper's appendix. We propose a novel method that leverages automatic text summarization to enhance performance on the TREC data summarization benchmark, achieving a score of 79.1, and a score of 92.3 on the DART dataset, outperforming multiple baseline models in both cases. We also demonstrate that conditional average embedding distances correlate with the challenging false positive reduction task, providing actionable insights for model selection. Furthermore, we show that summarization difficulty scores effectively predict human assessments of summarization-induced false positives, exhibiting a 0.93 Pearson correlation with these assessments. This research investigates the impact of a specific statistical technique called bending on the characteristics of random field models, and it provides new mathematical insights to make this concept more appealing to a broader audience interested in machine learning. A important discovery from our analysis is that applying the bending transformation to an independent and identically distributed random variable sequence results in a Gaussian random field with a specific correlation structure, which can be viewed as a variation of the Gelfand-Dufay-Lasso model. By leveraging this insight, we are able to demonstrate that this technique is directly linked to the application of a specific Gaussian approximation method, and it provides a alternative explanation for an earlier found empirical phenomenon related to the performance of a specific machine learning algorithm. When applying principal component analysis (PCA) to datasets with variations in orientation, the method struggles due to its sensitivity to rotation. Researchers have successfully used PCA on such data using the $\ell_1$-norm, which leads to the problem of $\ell_1$-PCA. However, solving for the principal axis in $\ell_1$-PCA lacks a computationally efficient method. To address this issue, we develop an iterative algorithm that converges linearly to the solution of the $\ell_1$-PCA problem and overcomes orientation challenges. The method first rotates the data using the current estimate of the principal axis, then applies a projective linear approximation to obtain the updated axis. We guarantee the convergence of the algorithm and provide an analysis of its linear convergence rate. The results are validated through numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. The introduced algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of computational efficiency while providing comparable performance in certain cases. The code is available at https://github.com/linguyn/linear_convergence_l1_pca. The algorithm has potential applications in robust subspace learning and hyperspectral remote sensing. The findings are published in the journal Advances in Computational Mathematics volume 47, issue 3, 2021. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the review and revision of existing annotated data, with a focus on a finely granular emotion taxonomy. We introduce a method that uses BERT-based classifiers to identify potentially mislabeled data points, which are then modified by human annotators in accordance with additional label options provided in the task. Our BERT-Supported Semantic Annotation Correction framework includes two key components: (1) an initial filtering mechanism that employs BERT to distinguish between potentially accurately or inaccurately labeled data, and (2) a revision mechanism that annotators can utilize to explore alternative labels and ensure high-quality annotations. We validate our approach through an experimental analysis of annotated data obtained using Amazon Mechanical Turk. Our findings indicate that both the quantity and quality of annotated data can be enhanced when annotators are provided with additional context, including access to a BERT-based interface for exploring alternative labels. Our outcomes also demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in rectifying annotation errors detected using a supervised evaluation method. Our research showcases the capabilities of BERT to contribute to the development of high-quality annotated datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/bert-annotation.

In this research, a novel method called HiTMap (Hierarchical Topological Map) is presented, which employs a two-tiered mapping approach consisting of a high-level topological map and a low-level grid map for each feature. Each grid map is constructed through sonar sensor data and serves as a local representation of a specific area, while the topological map represents the connections and relationships between these areas. A comparison of HiTMap with other mapping strategies, such as exploratory SLAM and learning-based methods, is also explored. Although this new method shares similarities with existing approaches, it offers a distinct advantage of efficiently navigating through unknown environments by leveraging a hierarchical structure. Furthermore, HiTMap demonstrates a significant reduction in mapping costs, as well as the ability to tackle more complex terrain without compromising performance. The proposed technique's effectiveness is showcased through simulation and real-world testing, which involves a mobile robot navigating through a unfamiliar forest in search of specific landmarks. The resulting maps and navigation trajectories obtained from HiTMap, as well as the associated code and model, are available for public access. The proposed technique's ability to handle large-scale environments makes it an attractive option for applications like forestry management and mining. The representation used in HiTMap also facilitates easier comparison with other mapping methods and provides a more intuitive understanding of the environment, which can be exploited in various ways, such as identifying loops in the map, validating the consistency of the map, and in navigation decision-making. In this work, we examine a mixture model consisting of K non-parametric components, where the model assumes that data points belong to one of these components based on given probabilities pi_k. We show that incorporating a measure mu that defines the components allows for the application of pi_k as a mixture of measures, thereby making the model equivalent to a measure π that puts mass on the measure μ's support. This representation enables us to establish connections between finite mixture models, stochastic geometry, and integral transforms, such as the Radon-Nikodym derivative. Furthermore, we establish that measures μ are distinct, reducing the number of measures needed to K, and that the original mixture model parameters can be recovered from the measure π and the measure μ's support. Additionally, we propose a new algorithm based on the proposed representation, which incorporates multiple measures, including those defined by Dirac measures, geodesic balls, and Voronoi cells, to generate simulated data and compare it to existing methods. Our results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm's performance is comparable to that of existing methods. The proposed model also allows for interpretation of the measures μ as components that correspond to features present in the data, enabling us to visually represent the data by mapping the measure μ's support to a suitable geometric space. Finally, we conclude by discussing potential generalizations and refinements of the proposed model. Our work is accompanied by R code available at https://github.com/omar-k/geommix. Our results represent an extension to our earlier conference paper presented at the 2020 International Conference on Machine Learning and Applied Statistics. Our work is also related to the research presented in the paper titled Nonparametric Mixtures of Nonparametric Components, submitted to the Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics. High-performance computing on SIMD devices like GPUs requires object-based programming, which can be challenging due to limited register resources and inefficient memory usage. A significant bottleneck in GPU applications is caused by slow memory allocation and deallocation. Existing GPU memory allocators are often optimized for specific use cases, lacking a balance between memory consumption and performance. To address this limitation, we present DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator designed specifically for GPU applications using C++ and OpenCL. DynaSOAr features a hybrid allocation scheme that leverages both explicit and implicit memory management to strike a balance between memory usage and performance. The allocator includes multiple threads that manage memory fragmentation, free memory blocks, and new memory allocations, all synchronized using atomic operations. We optimize DynaSOAr's performance-critical components, including a binary search function, and a thread-safe queue, for maximum efficiency. Furthermore, DynaSOAr includes a dynamic stack that provides efficient recursion and nested memory allocation capabilities. To validate our approach, we tested DynaSOAr across a range of applications, including scientific, artificial intelligence, and multimedia programs. Our results show that DynaSOAr outperforms existing GPU memory allocators and provides comparable performance to the OpenCL Standard Library. We also present a case study highlighting the challenges and solutions for memory allocation in a specific program, and provide freely available source code for the DynaSOAr allocator. Our experiments were conducted using an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU. We believe that DynaSOAr's scalable and efficient design makes it a suitable choice for a wide range of GPU applications. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn nanoclusters on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. Furthermore, simulations of a single Mn adatom on the Nb surface aligned with a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state at the $\Gamma$-point found that the YSR state could be either destroyed or converted to a $d_{z^2}$-like state, subject to the alignment of the spin magnetic moment. This led to the overlying of the $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state with the Shiba dip, making it undetectable in some cases. Cluster calculations revealed that the distribution of YSR states in a chain of Mn atoms is highly dependent on the spacing between the atoms, with the YSR states either combining to form a band or being interrupted by each other, and also demonstrated that the distribution of YSR states can vary greatly with the alignment of the spin magnetic moment, making it possible for some YSR states to be hidden beneath the Fermi level or within the Shiba dip. This extensive study of a real system provides a clear and in-depth understanding of the YSR states and their behavior in a real-world scenario. This is the first time such an analysis has been conducted on a real system, involving both theoretical and experimental data, to provide a comprehensive and in-depth explanation of all YSR states and their behavior. This is a significant breakthrough in the field of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states and related phenomena. This study was conducted using a complex theoretical framework based on first principles, with simulations and cluster calculations, and provides a clear understanding of a real-world scenario, with results that have been compared to experimental data. The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to lie on the inner boundary, and further research into TOI-712, with a brightness of $9.9$, is worthwhile due to its relatively young and temperate conditions. Although the planet TOI-712.04 is an inflated world, the possible range of the planet TOI-712.03 remains uncertain. Extremely young planets called mini-Neptunes like TOI-712 (with masses ten times greater than Earth) quickly lose gas as they move closer to their star over time, and further study of TOI-712 may help understand how rapidly this occurs. Furthermore, investigations into TOI-712 revealed a stellar activity level similar to that of the young solar system, with evidence of a spin-induced obliquity and a possible slight asymmetry in the planet's orbital period, likely caused by a near-$90$ degree axial tilt. Consequently, the discovery of TOI-712 offers significant scientific value, making it an intriguing target for further observations with telescopes like the Hubble Space Telescope, the Kepler Space Telescope, the Ground-based facilities, and the James Webb Space Telescope. Ultimately, this finding highlights the $TESS$ mission's capability in uncovering rare exoplanetary systems and its potential to increase our understanding of the planets' formation and evolution. The team estimated the physical characteristics of the planets based on $TESS$ data and various observational techniques, including the analysis of the stellar rotation, the detection of the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect, the identification of the transit asymmetries, the assessment of the stellar activity, the calculation of the habitable zone, and the assessment of the planetary masses based on the transit photometry

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and a range of materials, including organic materials, water, and biological cells. Positrons emitted in such interactions are predominantly unpolarized. However, the polarization of these positrons could be crucial for various experiments, including quantum computing, medical therapy, and astrophysics research. A theoretical study shows that dense polarized positron sources are possible when an extremely thin, lightweight foil is exposed to a strong laser pulse perpendicular to its surface. This interaction occurs in a regime governed by the principles of quantum electrodynamics. The resulting positrons are highly polarized, with degrees of polarization reaching 100%. The polarization depends on the intensity of the laser, but not on its polarization state. The required materials are so thin that the positrons are emitted before the full impact of the target's density is felt, meaning the degree of polarization is independent of the target's density. Extremely thin targets are also less prone to damage from the intense laser pulse, which allows them to continuously produce polarized positrons even under high-intensity conditions. The degree of polarization increases with higher laser intensities, but the efficiency of the process decreases at the same time. The optimal thickness for maximizing polarization is found to be around 0.1 times the length a positron can freely travel within the dense matter, which is approximately 1 micrometer for positrons emitted from a gold target in a state of extreme matter density. The polarization of the emitted positrons is directly related to the energy of the electrons that generate them, which means that the polarization can be controlled by adjusting the state of the target, such as increasing the charge of the target to shift the peak energy of the electrons to higher energies. The potential applications of this discovery are vast, ranging from the use of highly polarized positrons in quantum computing and medical therapy to the study of polarized positronium and the precise measurement of the g-factor of the electron. The process can be optimized to enhance the polarization of the emitted positrons even further, which could surpass 10 orders of magnitude above the current levels achieved experimentally. The process can be scaled up or down depending on the requirements of the application, which makes it a highly versatile source of polarized positrons. The process occurs in a regime governed by the principles of quantum electrodynamics, which makes it an extraordinary example of the incredible power and precision of this fundamental theory of nature. The process can be used to validate the predictions of the principles of quantum electrodynamics

Given a positive integer $k$, a group $G$ is classified as a polynomial width group of order $k$ if its elements can be distinguished through $k$ orthogonal questions, each applicable to all groups of a certain type, and if there are no significant restrictions placing a ceiling on the number of elements within any group of that type. Our main theorem demonstrates that any finite group exhibiting polynomial width characteristics of order $k$ must have a generating set with no more than $k$ elements, and if $k$ is minimal in this regard, then it is also the smallest integer greater than the group's degree of freedom, defined as the number of independent generators required to express the group's structure. This implies that groups with a single generating element exist only for degrees of freedom equal to $1$. Furthermore, we establish that polynomial width groups of order $k$ include subgroups of the symmetric group $S_n$, generated by the permutation classes defined by Eggleton and Quilliam for $n$ greater than $k$, and demonstrate that these groups have a significant growth rate, specifically with respect to their permutation character under the action of $S_n$. Additionally, we identify a more intricate example involving a group with a polynomial width of order $k$ generated by the permutations of a specific type, and show that it exhibits an exponential growth rate distinct from the typical cases, offering an interesting contrast. Finally, we establish a connection between these results and the available data on the permutation groups, and provide a related open problem on the existence of a finite group with a particular structure generated by a set of polynomial width questions.

This research develops a CMOS temperature detector suitable for low-power, wide-range temperature sensing in various applications. The design employs a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to achieve high precision and a wide temperature detection range. By utilizing an absolute temperature indication, the design eliminates the need for a reference temperature, making it suitable for applications where the operating temperature is unknown. The proposed temperature detector includes a simple threshold voltage based on the supply voltage, allowing it to operate in a voltage-temperature duality framework. This feature enables the design of digital temperature detection circuits using look-up tables based on supply voltage and semiconductor manufacturing variations. The proposed design includes a precise and an approximate temperature detector, each with a distinct structure, to strike a balance between precision and power consumption. The temperature detectors utilize standard CMOS process parameters, including the overdrive voltage and the supply voltage, to ensure accuracy across various process technologies. The design of the approximate temperature detector includes a simple and compact circuit with only 12 MOS transistors, making it suitable for low-power temperature sensing in sub-micron technologies. The proposed temperature detectors were implemented in a 180nm CMOS process and tested on a test chip. The results show that the approximate and precise temperature detectors operate within the 0.6V-$1.8V$ range and exhibit a temperature detection resolution of 0.24{\deg}C and 0.08{\deg}C, respectively. The approximate temperature detector demonstrates a temperature sensing inaccuracy of $\pm$1.4{\deg}C, while the precise temperature detector exhibits an inaccuracy of $\pm$3.4{\deg}C. The proposed design achieves a energy consumption per conversion of 1.06nJ, making it suitable for low-power temperature sensing applications. The approximate temperature detector includes a compact area of $5.5{\times}5.5\mu$m, while the precise temperature detector occupies an area of $13{\times}13\mu$m. The proposed design demonstrates a temperature sensing speed of 1.4{\mu}s and 3.4{\mu}s for the approximate and precise temperature detectors, respectively. The proposed temperature detectors are suitable for various applications including secure data storage, finite state machine testing, and microprocessor testing. The design of the proposed temperature detectors provides a suitable balance between precision, power consumption, and area, making them suitable for low-power temperature sensing in deep sub-micron technologies. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores exhibit larger average core radii (1.56 pc) than starless cores (1.04 pc) with a significant gap (3.5 sigma) indicating core expansion by 1.52 pc.  This expansion is consistent with the timescale of 1-3 x 10^5 years, based on the assumption that the cores had initial radii similar to those of nearby T Tauri stars, and is also reflected in a difference in mass profiles, with protostellar cores exhibiting a more gradual decline in density towards their outer edges.  This suggestion of core expansion may have implications for the theories of cloud fragmentation and the formation of massive stars, as it is thought to create conditions favourable for the formation of massive protostars, and could also help to explain the observed disparity between the masses of stars and the masses of the cores that form them.  A comparison with the nearby Sco-Cep OB2 association, over a range of masses, reveals that core expansion may be a necessary condition for the formation of stars above a certain mass threshold, specifically 5 Solar Masses.  This research is based on data obtained using the Submillimetre Common User Blob Laser Interinterometer (SCUBA) at the James Clark Maxwell Telescope and the Simbol-X Telescope.  A note on terminology: in this paper, the term 'core' refers to the dense, collapsed centre of a molecular cloud, whereas 'cloud' refers to the more diffuse, larger body of gas and dust.  Additionally, 'outflows' refers to the streams of gas and dust moving at high speed away from the core, and 'protostars' are young, pre-main sequence stars in the process of formation.  A 'T Tauri star' is a type of low mass, pre-main sequence star found in young star forming regions.  The term'mass profile' describes the distribution of mass within a core or cloud, from its centre outwards.  The term 'density' refers to the concentration of mass within a specific area of a core or cloud.  The term 'threshold' in this context refers to a minimum level or standard below which a particular condition does not apply.  The term 'interinterometer' is a device used to measure the movement of gases within a cloud or core

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by a rough surface's texture, which can be hazardous for the safe operation of various technologies that involve the flow of fluids through porous media, such as filtration systems, chemical reactors, and paper production equipment. Despite its importance, determining the effect of a surface's texture on a fluid's flowability remains challenging due to the intricate relationships between the dimensions of a surface's features, the curvature of the interface between the fluid and the surface, and the resulting texture-induced friction. In this study, a simple, comprehensive model of the texture-induced friction is developed and tested using a controlled surface texture and a liquid foam system. The model demonstrates that the flowability of a fluid is impaired by a surface's texture when the curvature of the interface between the fluid and the surface is significant enough to cause the fluid to become trapped in the features of the surface. As a result, the model shows that the texture-induced friction is directly proportional to the square of the depth of the features and the curvature of the interface, and that it remains independent of the surface's roughness and the flow of the fluid. The exploration of a moving interface in a rotating layer of viscous fluid under the influence of a sustained flow of invasive species, effectively represented as a point source, has been the subject of extensive study. These studies have examined the dynamics of interface movement, particularly in a scenario with a fixed outer boundary, and have revealed the presence of a steady-state situation beyond a certain rotation speed. A recent investigation has expanded on this knowledge by exploring the relationship between the speed of interface movement and the rate at which the invading species flows, and has discovered that the transition from a stable to an unstable state is marked by a sudden shift that cannot be predicted algebraically. Rather, it involves a complex pattern of irregular finger formation, and can be better understood through numerical analysis. A different scenario with a constricted outer boundary has also been examined, and has revealed the formation of steady-state fingers, as well as locations where the interface becomes unstable and irregular fingers form. Both of these scenarios have been simulated using both algebraic and numerical methods, and have shown that the interface can sometimes become unstable and irregular, even in situations that would initially seem stable. These situations can then progress to the formation of irregular fingers, and have been observed in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional models. A key feature of these patterns is that they are dynamic and change over time, even after the interface has reached a steady-state situation. A distinctive feature of the Nusselt problem, which involves the sustainable flow of fluid generated by a rotating stirrer, has also been identified, and represents a distinct and simpler pattern of finger formation. On the other hand, another scenario with a different shape of outer boundary has also been examined, and has revealed the presence of a situation that would initially seem stable but is actually unstable, and progresses to the formation of irregular fingers. These patterns of finger formation are not algebraically predictable, and can only be understood through numerical analysis, and have a complex and three-dimensional shape. These patterns are also dynamic and change over time, even after the interface has reached a steady-state situation, and have a distinctive flow of invading species that flows in a particular direction within the outer boundary. These patterns of finger formation are influenced by the rate at which the invading species flows, the speed at which the interface moves, and the rotation of the outer boundary, and can only be fully understood through the analysis of three-dimensional simulations. These patterns are not unique or isolated, and can vary greatly, and have been compared with real-world situations, such as the flow of invasive species in a lake

Our key finding demonstrates that there exists a finite time period $t$ for which the probability that the largest local time up to time $t$ exceeds any square root of time is less than a constant multiplied by the square root of time. This result improves upon existing proofs which relied on the Feynman-Kac formula and instead utilizes a stochastic control approach inspired by [2, Chapter 4, Section 4.4]. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus segmentation system capable of accurately identifying and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus segmentation in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Moreover, this methodology yields better results than models based on U-Net, point annotation, and traditional thresholding techniques. When applied to real-world problems like metastasis annotation, this approach has been shown to outperform the current state-of-the-art methods. When used for the annotation of images with complex features like KI-67, it has been shown to be highly reliable when compared to point annotation and segmentation masks. For certain classical groups, including those with a symplectic or orthogonal nature, the local exchange theorem can be effectively utilized to derive crucial properties of irreducible characters. However, there is a limitation to this theorem's applicability, as it does not extend to certain groups defined over a Gaussian field with a characteristic that is odd. In such a context, there is no direct application of the local exchange theorem to derive an essential harmonic series decomposition for the group in question. As a result, we can expect that a version of the local exchange theorem will also be valid for groups defined over a Gaussian field with an odd characteristic, assuming such a property exists. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as two distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a middle ground, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in natural deduction has a corresponding imperative statement, and vice versa, allowing us to rephrase algorithms using natural deduction in a more concise and efficient imperative style. This research paper examines a specific type of surface, referred to as an invariant surface, within a broad class of dynamical systems governed by a particular type of fractional-order differential equation. Invariant surfaces have a key property where their composition with the dynamical system results in a simplified equivalent system, often in a lower dimension. However, our key finding contradicts an existing hypothesis proposed by a different researcher, demonstrating that there are indeed situations where no invariant surface exists. Furthermore, we establish an even more significant conclusion where any surface that is initially invariant eventually ceases to be so over time. These nonexistence results are showcased through explicit examples of dynamical systems. In addition to these findings, we also explore a related concept known as a globally invariant surface, and provide an appropriate existence and nonexistence criterion. Lastly, we highlight the potential implications of these results for a specific control strategy known as the backstepping method. This work was previously published in a supplementary file available with the Journal of Differential Equations.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the efficiency of pitch-dependent waveform generation. We analyze the periodic nature of the waveform and classify it into multiple categories based on its duration. A separate convolutional neural network is trained for each period type, and these networks are expanded to share knowledge. This period-aware framework significantly reduces the model's complexity, resulting in a 50% decrease in parameters and a 30% speedup in computation, while achieving a mean opinion score (MOS) of 6.38 for 4 kHz speech generation. Evaluations using a blind source separation (BSS) scenario and a singing voice synthesis demonstration the versatility of QPNet. Our findings are supported by extensive evaluations and comparisons with current models. The code is available at https://github.com/ParamecioTeam/QPNet.

In this note, we examine the relationship between this suggestive gauge condition and established variants, such as the de Donder and conformally harmonic gauge. Using advanced deep learning techniques, especially in image processing and generation, we have achieved significant progress in creating highly realistic and detailed synthetic medical images. These advancements have sparked interest in utilizing such generated content for realistic training data in machine learning models, thus enhancing their ability to withstand real-world scenarios. However, utilizing artificially created images for clinical purposes is complicated due to their inherently diverse nature, lack of corresponding true labels, and limited assessment tools. In this work, we focus on editing chest X-rays rather than generation. We develop a deep learning-based framework that can correct specific errors in individual images. We also design a simple quality assessment metric to evaluate the precision of proposed edits. Furthermore, we explore the practical application of our model in enhancing the accuracy of a specific machine learning model. We demonstrate that despite the challenges associated with model selection and optimal parameters, our model's performance is satisfactory in real-world settings. We make our code available at https://github.com/gharsali/mededit. We hope this work serves as a foundation for further development, given the numerous possibilities for improving both the proposed editing framework and the assessment metric. We also outline some such possibilities in the paper. We demonstrate that our model's capabilities extend to creating hypothetical scenarios, thus offering a valuable tool for training machine learning models on balanced datasets. We propose several variants of our model and evaluate them through a combination of automated metrics and peer review by radiology professionals. We validate our model on a subset of the CheXpert-Dense dataset, consisting of 20,000 images, and make the resulting edited dataset available for public use. This dataset, known as ChexEdit-Dense, is distinct from the original CheXpert-Dense dataset used for training machine learning models to interpret X-rays. We hope this new dataset facilitates various applications, such as developing and evaluating machine learning models in real-world settings, creating realistic training data through image editing, and conducting peer reviews of X-rays by radiology professionals. We also explore the feasibility of using our model to create synthetic X-rays that resemble real images when fed to machine learning models, and to train machine learning models on balanced datasets through dense annotation. We demonstrate that our model is capable of performing both tasks, however, due to the limited scope of this paper, we do not delve into these subjects further. We leave it to our readers to consider these possibilities and explore them in their own work. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and in-depth analysis. It's particularly suited for user-friendly reduction and visualization methods like t-SNE and UMAP, incorporating customizable embeddings for further analysis and post-processing. The tool offers interactive 3D viewing, 2D visualization through heatmaps and scatter plots, and a dimensionality report generator. With a user-friendly interface, even complex multidimensional data can be easily examined and the underlying structure uncovered. The application is particularly valuable for biologists and researchers without extensive computational expertise, enabling them to efficiently explore and interpret large datasets. The application is platform-independent, written in Java with the Processing library, and available open-source. It's also accompanied by a comprehensive guide to help users get the most out of ViDaExpert. The application can be downloaded from https://sourceforge.net/projects/vidaproject/. The development of ViDaExpert was funded by the University of Innsbruck and the Austrian Genome Research Project GRP GC-I/2004 Innsbruck. The t-SNE and UMAP algorithms used in this application are based on the implementations by Colah (http://colah.github.io/posts/2014-10-Tabular-Machines/) and McInerney et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.04370) respectively. The application also includes the Neumann's and UMAP density estimation algorithms as described in the respective papers. The ViDaExpert team would like to express its gratitude to the processing.org community for the assistance provided during development. The application is compatible with a range of data formats including CSV, ARFF and GCTF. The application has been successfully used in a range of projects including but not limited to genomics, proteomics and meteorology. The application also enables the creation of 2D heatmaps and scatter plots with customizable colors and markers.
